name: Oberheim DMX
originalPurpose: A programmable drum machine for studios and bands, built on short digital recordings of real drums stored on memory chips rather than on synthesised tones. The chips could be swapped for other sounds.
whatActuallyHappened: In Queens, producer Larry Smith programmed a drummer's pattern into one and built Run-D.M.C.'s first single around it with almost nothing else. The DMX's hard, bright hits, soaked in reverb, became the sound of the rap records that came after the Sugar Hill house-band era. The same machine also drove pop and new wave records of the early 1980s.
priceStory: List price was about 2,900 US dollars in 1980 to 1981, comparable to its rival the LinnDrum. This was a studio purchase, not a bedroom one, so its place in rap came through producers with studio access rather than through cheap secondhand units the way the 808 arrived.
hook: The drum machine behind the first Run-D.M.C. record, which threw out the band and left rap with nothing but drums and voices.
blurb: The DMX was one of the first drum machines to play short digital recordings of real drums instead of making drum sounds out of electronics, which made it hit harder and sound more real than older machines. It sits between two eras on this map. Its sounds were sampled, like the SP-1200's, but came built in on chips rather than recorded by the user, so a producer arranged sounds rather than choosing them. In 1983 a producer named Larry Smith used one to make Run-D.M.C.'s first record, 'Sucker M.C.'s'. He left out the band completely: just the drum machine and two rappers. That broke with the house-band model Sugar Hill had set, and made the drum machine the whole track rather than a stand-in for a drummer. After that, rap records started sounding bare and hard instead of like disco with talking on top. The end year here comes from a single secondary source and is not confirmed elsewhere.
